I'm building with native-dates, a date library on the browser's Temporal and Intl APIs. Read this docs page: {url}

Summarize what it teaches in one short paragraph and a few bullets, assuming I haven't read it. Then ask me what I'm building and what I want to learn, and answer from the documentation.

home.description: Your browser’s native dates in plain English. A thin date library on Temporal and Intl: four nouns, plain verbs and frozen values.
home.hero.title: Your browser’s native dates in plain English
home.hero.lede: Temporal gave the browser real time zones, daylight saving and calendar math. Native Dates gives it an API to match: four nouns, verbs you can read aloud and values that never change under you, in {size} br.
home.say.caption: Each column is one thought. Turn a phrase, and everything after it follows.
home.prims.title: Built on the primitives Temporal ships
home.prims.lede: JavaScript now has a real type for a calendar day, a time of day, a moment in a time zone and a length of time. Native Dates hands you each one in a call short enough to remember.
home.prims.datetime: A moment in a time zone
home.consoles.title: Date gets these wrong. Temporal gets them right.
home.consoles.lede: Four questions every app asks. Date has answered them the same way since 1995. Ask one, and see what each says.
home.consoles.day.ask: What day is 2026-09-01 in New York?
home.consoles.day.why: Date reads a bare date as midnight in UTC, which is still the evening before in New York. A calendar date has no clock to shift, so it is September 1 everywhere.
home.consoles.month.ask: What is one month after January 31?
home.consoles.month.why: Date counts to February 31 and spills into March. Temporal stops at the last day February has.
home.consoles.clocks.ask: It is 9 AM on Saturday in New York. What time is it one day later?
home.consoles.clocks.why: The clocks spring forward that night, so the day is 23 hours long. Outside its own zone, Date can only add 24 hours. Temporal adds a day and keeps the clock at nine.
home.consoles.start.ask: The due date is 30 days after the start. What is the start now?
home.consoles.start.why: setDate() changes the date it is called on, and due is the same object as start. A Temporal value never changes, so plus() hands back a new one.
home.year.title: Every zone and every clock change, already in your browser
home.year.lede: Los Angeles and Berlin change their clocks on different weekends, so the hours between them change {changes} a year. Date knows two zones, yours and UTC. Temporal knows every zone on every date, so a standup set in one city lands at the right time in the other.
home.year.caption: A 9:30 standup in Los Angeles, read in Berlin on every day of {year}. On {days} the two cities are {near} hours apart instead of {far}, and it starts at {time}.
home.xray.title: Code you can read aloud
home.xray.lede: Every call is one word for one thought, in the order you would say it. Switch to Temporal to read the same dates written against the platform.
home.xray.label: Show the code
home.xray.note: Both programs give the same three results. The build that made this page ran them to check.
home.xray.fact.words: One word per thought next('monday') finds the day, and at() gives it a time and a place. On Temporal that is weekday arithmetic and an options bag.
home.xray.fact.zones: A zone is a view in() reads the same moment on another clock, and format('full') writes it the way the reader’s locale does.
home.xray.fact.calendar: Calendar math by name endOf('month') is the 28th, the 30th or the 31st, without asking how long the month is.
home.xray.fact.durations: Durations in words until() reads both moments in one zone, and format() prints the wait in the reader’s language.
home.try.title: Run it as if you were in Tokyo
home.try.lede: A small app, built and run in your browser. Pick a zone in the preview’s bar and it runs as it would there. Change the code and it rebuilds as you type.
home.try.label: Live example: a meeting across zones
home.bytes.title: The whole core is {size}
home.bytes.lede: Four nouns, every verb, formatting and zones, with no dependencies. A plugin adds one more thing when you import it. Switch them on to see what your app would ship.

examples.title: Examples · native-dates
examples.lede: Small apps you can run and edit right here. Each one shows one thing the library does, with a few things to try in the preview.
plugins.title: Plugins · native-dates
plugins.lede: The core covers what nearly every app does with a date. Each plugin adds one more thing when you import it, so you ship only the ones you use. Select the ones you want and copy the setup.

plugins.view.label: Show plugins as
plugins.callout.title: Need something else?
plugins.callout.body: A plugin is a module you import: it adds methods to the four nouns and wraps the ones already there. Writing a plugin covers how.
plugins.preset.full.description: Every plugin, for when size is not the question.
plugins.preset.scheduling.description: Spans and city names, for apps that book time across zones.
plugins.preset.compat.description: Token formats, relative time, loose reading and the `Date` getters, for code arriving from Day.js or Moment.
plugins.ranges.description: Spans between two dates, datetimes or times, with `to()`, `contains()`, `overlaps()` and `points()`.
plugins.tokens.description: Token patterns such as `YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm` in `format()`, as Day.js and Moment write them.
plugins.relative.description: `formatRelative()`: “in 3 days” or “3 hours ago”, in the reader’s language.
plugins.zones.description: Zones by city, `'Berlin'`, by abbreviation, `'PT'`, and by names of your own.
plugins.loose.description: Reads what `Date` reads, such as `'March 5, 2026'`, and gives `null` for what can’t be read.
plugins.legacy-date.description: The `Date` getters, `getFullYear()` and the rest, on a datetime, for code that still calls them.
